question: When a nonconvex lower-level objective has many possibly degenerate critical points, what well-defined game do practical warm-started bilevel algorithms solve, and can their biased unrolled hypergradients be corrected?

key_findings.claim: A critical-point selection map makes an otherwise ambiguous nonconvex bilevel interaction well-defined by encoding how the leader anticipates the follower's optimizer-dependent choice.
key_findings.evidence: The map takes the current upper and lower variables to a lower-level critical point and must leave an existing critical point fixed. Composing the upper loss with this map defines a Bilevel Game with Selection; when the lower minimizer is unique it reduces to ordinary bilevel optimization, while retaining the previous lower state permits warm starts.

key_findings.claim: For a smooth coercive parametric Morse-Bott lower loss, continuous gradient flow defines a locally differentiable selection even along a manifold of degenerate local minima.
key_findings.evidence: The parametric Morse-Bott lemma preserves local critical-point type as the upper parameter varies and yields a locally uniform Lojasiewicz inequality. Under global lower-gradient Lipschitzness and coercivity, the flow converges; near a selected local minimum its derivative converges uniformly and the selection derivative at a critical initialization is the mixed Hessian times the Moore-Penrose inverse of the lower Hessian.

key_findings.claim: Finite-step unrolling generally converges, if it converges at all, to a stationary point of an approximate game rather than the exact selection game.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 3 is conditional on convergence of the iterates and assumes uniform convergence of both the unrolled map and its derivative near local minima. It makes the exact selection residual vanish only as the number of unrolled steps tends to infinity. The synthetic quadratic shows small unroll counts reaching a wrong stationary point while 1,000 steps approach the chosen equilibrium more slowly.

key_findings.claim: A pseudoinverse-based implicit-gradient correction removes the finite-unrolling bias at any convergent local-minimum limit under the paper's assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: The correction subtracts the mixed-Hessian/lower-Hessian-pseudoinverse term from the unrolled hypergradient and can approximate it using Hessian-vector products plus warm-started least squares. Proposition 5 says any convergent joint sequence of upper, lower, and solver states is a first-order BGS equilibrium if the lower limit is a local minimizer, without sending the unroll length to infinity.

anchors.section: D.1-D.2 warm starts and recovered algorithms

key_findings.claim: The CIFAR-10 dataset-distillation experiment is promising but too thin to validate the theory for modern deep-learning bilevel problems.
key_findings.evidence: With one unrolled ResNet-18 update and 100 synthetic images, the corrected run ends at 54.19% test accuracy versus 48.6% without correction while training accuracy is similar. The paper gives one curve, no seeds, error bars, compute accounting, code link, alternative hypergradient baselines, or check that the neural loss satisfies the parametric Morse-Bott and smoothness assumptions.

anchors.section: E.2 Dataset Distillation on CIFAR10 and Figure 4

key_findings.claim: The results characterize a chosen optimizer-dependent first-order game, not a solution of the original optimistic, pessimistic, or global-minimizer bilevel program.
key_findings.evidence: A selection need only return a critical point and is self-consistent even at a saddle; equilibrium is defined by vanishing first derivatives. The flow-selection theory becomes differentiable near local minima, but the algorithms' exactness statements remain conditional on convergence to such a limit. Different selections or practical discrete optimizers can therefore define different games and outcomes.

key_findings.claim: The paper's assertion that the parametric Morse-Bott class covers practical machine-learning models is not established for the neural experiment.
key_findings.evidence: The global theory assumes at least three continuous derivatives, a globally Lipschitz lower gradient, coercivity, locally constant critical-manifold rank/type, and exact gradient flow. The examples proved to satisfy the structural assumption are nondegenerate smooth functions and diffeomorphic deformations of Morse-Bott functions. ReLU ResNet-18 is nonsmooth, and no theorem or empirical rank audit connects its loss to this class.

method.core_idea: Make lower-solution multiplicity explicit through an optimizer-induced selection, differentiate that selection along a degenerate critical manifold, and correct the mismatch between finite unrolling and the limiting selection hypergradient.
method.mechanism: Define BGS from a critical, self-consistent map; instantiate the map as infinite-time lower gradient flow; use a parameterized Morse-Bott normal form and a uniform Lojasiewicz inequality to prove convergence, continuity, and differentiability; express the derivative with a Hessian pseudoinverse; add its missing component to iterative differentiation using warm-started Hessian-vector least squares.
assumptions: The lower objective is at least three-times continuously differentiable and parametric Morse-Bott around every augmented critical point.
The lower gradient is globally Lipschitz in the lower variable and the lower objective is coercive for each upper variable.
The selected continuous gradient-flow limit is a local minimum rather than a saddle or maximum.
Discrete unrolled maps and their upper derivatives converge uniformly to the selected flow near local minima.
The algorithm's upper, lower, and auxiliary least-squares iterates converge to a limit.
Hessian-vector products and a stable minimum-norm pseudoinverse approximation are computationally available.

techniques.role: Encodes the lower optimizer's choice among many critical points.
Keeps the local critical-manifold geometry stable as upper variables vary.
Constructs a self-consistent selection from continuous lower gradient flow.
Extends implicit differentiation to singular lower Hessians.
Adds a least-squares Hessian-vector correction to finite-step iterative differentiation.

evaluations.setting: A 2,000-dimensional upper and 1,000-dimensional lower quadratic game with a 100-dimensional lower Hessian null space.
evaluations.metric: Distance to a closed-form BGS equilibrium and approximate hypergradient norm versus wall-clock time
evaluations.result: Uncorrected T at most 10 converges to a point more than 10^3 away in the reported metric, T=1,000 approaches the equilibrium slowly, and corrected T at most 10 recovers it faster.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 distilled to 100 learned images with ResNet-18 and one lower gradient step.
evaluations.metric: Training and test accuracy over time
evaluations.result: The corrected run reports 54.19% final test accuracy versus 48.6% without correction, with similar training accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: The same unrolled algorithm without the implicit correction; no repeated-run uncertainty or stronger distillation baseline is reported.

limitations: Reviewer inference: parametric Morse-Bott regularity is strong, local, and unverified for the nonsmooth deep network used experimentally.
Reviewer inference: the exact algorithmic propositions assume convergence instead of proving it and supply no finite-time rate for the corrected method.
Reviewer inference: a selection can choose any critical point, so BGS need not solve a lower global optimum or even a stable local optimum outside the qualified theorem setting.
Reviewer inference: continuous gradient-flow selection may differ from SGD, momentum, Adam, finite-step schedules, stochastic noise, and restart behavior.
Reviewer inference: the pseudoinverse correction adds second-order products, solver state, conditioning sensitivity, and hyperparameters whose cost is not benchmarked.
Reviewer inference: the only deep-learning result is one CIFAR-10 curve with no seeds, error bars, code, compute, or matched modern baselines.
Reviewer inference: constrained, nonsmooth, stochastic, and noncoercive cases are explicitly left open.
failure_modes: A parameter perturbation can turn a minimum manifold into saddles, making the selection discontinuous as illustrated by Figure 2.
Critical-manifold rank changes or intersections violate the parametric Morse-Bott condition and invalidate the pseudoinverse sensitivity formula.
Finite unrolling can reach a zero approximate hypergradient far from the intended BGS equilibrium.
An ill-conditioned nonzero Hessian spectrum can make the least-squares correction noisy or expensive.
Stochastic lower optimization can jump between basins, so no deterministic self-consistent selection describes its behavior.
Convergence to a saddle satisfies the selection definition and first-order conditions but may be unstable or useless.
reusable_insights: State the lower-solution selection rule as part of any underdetermined bilevel problem; otherwise the mathematical objective is incomplete.
Distinguish the target hypergradient from the gradient of a finite unroll, even when both vanish at an algorithmic fixed point.
Use pseudoinverse sensitivity only after auditing constant rank, local solution type, and conditioning along the selected manifold.
Benchmark correction accuracy per unit time and memory, not only final outer performance.
Treat optimizer, initialization, warm start, stochasticity, and restart policy as components of the learned solution concept.
open_questions: Can comparable selection differentiability be proved for discrete stochastic optimizers with momentum or Adam?
How can one test the parametric Morse-Bott or constant-rank premise in a large neural network without constructing its Hessian?
What nonasymptotic rate and oracle complexity does the corrected algorithm achieve under realistic approximate solves?
How should a selection be chosen when basin stability, validation performance, fairness, or robustness are competing criteria?
Can the construction handle nonsmooth networks, constraints, regularizers, and basin bifurcations?
Does the correction improve modern data reweighting, architecture search, meta-learning, or RL at matched compute across many seeds?

competitive_landscape.title: On Implicit Bias in Overparameterized Bilevel Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Vicol et al. empirically and analytically distinguish cold-start and warm-start equilibria and show strong dependence on the hypergradient approximation. The present paper formalizes this algorithm dependence as a selection game and derives a singular-Hessian correction under Morse-Bott assumptions.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Gradient-based Bilevel Optimization with Non-convex Followers and Beyond
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. use initialization auxiliaries and pessimistic trajectory truncation to approximate nonconvex follower solutions with convergence guarantees. BGS instead embraces the optimizer's selected critical point and studies its differentiability, targeting a different solution concept.

competitive_landscape.title: On Penalty Methods for Nonconvex Bilevel Optimization and First-Order Stochastic Approximation
competitive_landscape.difference: Kwon et al. approximate the original hyper-objective with a penalty formulation, provide a multiple-solution gradient formula under error-bound conditions, and give nonasymptotic first-order stochastic complexities. It avoids an explicit optimizer selection map but targets solution-set optimality rather than an algorithm-defined game.

competitive_landscape.title: Moreau Envelope for Nonconvex Bi-Level Optimization: A Single-loop and Hessian-free Solution Strategy
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. use a Moreau-envelope reformulation and a first-order, Hessian-free single loop with nonasymptotic guarantees and broader application experiments. That is more scalable than pseudoinverse correction, while BGS gives a more explicit account of optimizer-selected degenerate manifolds.

competitive_landscape.title: Select-then-differentiate: Solving Bilevel Optimization with Manifold Lower-level Solution Sets
competitive_landscape.difference: Masiha et al. explicitly select an optimistic solution on a lower-minimizer manifold, derive a pseudoinverse hypergradient and regularity limits under local PL conditions, and give intrinsic-dimension convergence plus matched-budget LLM data-reweighting results. It strengthens practical validation and optimization guarantees but chooses an upper-aware optimistic selection rather than the follower's flow-induced one.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Selection maps resolve nonconvex bilevel ambiguity, a parametric Morse-Bott analysis extends implicit differentiation to degenerate critical points, and an implicit correction removes finite-unrolling bias.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper develops a parameterized Morse-Bott normal form, convergence and sensitivity results for gradient-flow selections, conditional fixed-point theorems for corrected unrolling, a closed-form singular quadratic, and one dataset-distillation demonstration.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The selection-game formalization and degenerate-manifold sensitivity analysis are substantial theoretical contributions. Their practical reach is uncertain because the assumptions are unverified for the neural example, exactness is conditional on convergence, and later penalty, Moreau, and select-then-differentiate methods offer explicit complexity or broader experiments.
